candidate.educational_objective: Respond to compression-device discomfort after arthroplasty by assessing and escalating the concern without independently abandoning prescribed VTE prophylaxis or ordered mobilization.

options.A: Remove the compression device for the remainder of the shift and rely on the prescribed anticoagulant because pharmacologic prophylaxis replaces mechanical methods.
options.B: Leave the compression device off until the surgeon rounds, keep the client in bed, and avoid ambulation because walking may worsen calf discomfort or reveal an unrecognized thrombus.
options.C: Pause the device, assess the calf and the prescribed prophylaxis plan, report the discomfort, and continue ordered mobilization if it is safe.
options.D: Reduce the device pressure below the prescribed setting and use it only while the client sleeps, because partial overnight compression provides equivalent prophylaxis.

candidate.rationale: A prior DVT places an arthroplasty client at increased VTE risk. AAOS arthroplasty guidance supports risk-appropriate multimodal prevention that includes mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis with early mobilization. Calf discomfort should be assessed and reported rather than used as a reason to abandon prescribed prophylaxis, keep the client on bed rest, or independently change device settings. If the device cannot be used safely, the prophylaxis plan should be reassessed by the care team.
candidate.source_claim_supported: A prior DVT raises VTE risk after total joint arthroplasty; risk-appropriate prophylaxis uses mechanical and pharmacologic measures with early mobilization, so discomfort warrants assessment/escalation rather than unilateral discontinuation or device-setting changes.
